claims.text: The starting material is a conventional single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeNi alloy.
Adding approximately 2–5 at.% Ti to CoCrFeNi will induce stable, fine nanoprecipitates.
The additive will produce an ultrafine-grained matrix containing dispersed, coherent nanoprecipitates.
The resulting nanohierarchical architecture will adaptively protect the sliding interface from room temperature through 800 °C.
At room temperature, coupled nanoscale grains and precipitates will relieve frictional stress through multiple deformation pathways.
At elevated temperature, the nanoprecipitates will trigger formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer.
The nanocrystalline glaze layer will minimize adhesive and oxidative wear at temperatures up to 800 °C.
The Ti-modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the full temperature range.
The Ti-modified alloy will have a reduced wear rate, potentially by an order of magnitude, relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the full temperature range.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has difficulty maintaining low friction and wear at high temperature.
The proposed mechanism is operative in ambient air under sliding loads from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
Identically processing the base and Ti-modified specimens provides a controlled comparison of the alloying intervention.
Coefficient of friction and wear rate will be measured at room temperature and 800 °C.
TEM and SEM will be used to assess grain size, nanoprecipitate distribution, and formation of the surface glaze layer.

The hypothesis is declared falsified only if the modified alloy lacks a statistically significant friction and wear reduction and also lacks the proposed nanohierarchical structure and high-temperature glaze.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims performance continuously across approximately 25–800 °C, but the proposed experiment tests only the two endpoints while treating the result as a test across the entire range.
